utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, please continue your cross-examination. Can I have an indication, Mr. Tapuskovic, of how long you will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you for giving me the floor. Yesterday afternoon and this morning, I used my time to keep cutting back my questions, and I think I will take a lot less time to complete my cross-examination than the Prosecutor originally took to examine the witness in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sir, yesterday the last thing we spoke about was the UNPROFOR report dated the 18th of June. Some other questions related to that report before I tender the document as a Defence exhibit. Is it true what the report says, that the UNMOs were not allowed to visit the hospitals since the 15th of June, 1995? Is this true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about any ban on UNMOs visiting hospitals. It's the very first I hear of it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not me claiming it. It's the UNMO report. It's the UNPROFOR report; it's the UNPROFOR people who are claiming this, not me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I hear of it, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He said he knows nothing about it, so please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the BH army offensive, along all confrontation lines, got off the ground on the 15th of June? Can you confirm that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't confirm that. I didn't deal with things like that. My job was an entirely different one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I just want to ensure that counsel turns off his microphone when the witness is answering. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe there is a system in place for it to be turned off automatically, is there not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand the primary control remains with counsel, although the AV booth can override. So it is your responsibility, Mr. Tapuskovic, to turn off the mic when you're not speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm putting it to you that that was not allowed because, for the most part, victims of the armed conflict were in hospitals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Victims of the armed conflict in Sarajevo, as never before in history, were for the most part civilians. The greatest number of casualties was among the civilian population, and that's the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that you conducted an investigation of the Simone Bolivar school incident, you must know that on this particular occasion UNPROFOR were granted permission to access the hospital and inspect the victims of the June 18th incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this permission or the fact that they went there and inspected the victims, I know nothing about that. We had nothing to do with that. We just determined the equipment and the weapons used and the azimuth; that is, where the shells were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can 65 ter document 00532 please be admitted as a Defence exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D73, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, yesterday I showed you 65 ter document 113. This is an official report. I read back to you the following portion: "All the evidence found was preserved and photographed. The scene of crime was sketched and photographed." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw many of those sketches and photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have photograph P257 brought up for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These are the two photographs that the Prosecutor showed you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in this first photograph you marked the spot, the exact point of impact of the projectile, and then the shrapnel flew back towards the positions that you marked hitting a considerable number of people, blowing their heads off. Many of them were killed and some were seriously wounded. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Look at this place, sir. There's some white surface there, something white on the ground. I see some glasses. Could that possibly be paper, sheets of paper? There is not a single blood-mark in this place. Can you explain that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever you had mass murder and massacres, blood-marks would be removed once the investigation was over, or maybe it had to be removed for the traces of the shell to be identified. So this is no paper and no paper sheets. This is light coming from outside. And these are not buckets; these are jerrycans that people used to fetch water.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you are saying that did you not take any photographs of those persons as you found them, nor did you take any photographs of the horror that you found, having arrived at the scene.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found a lot of blood and body parts before they were removed, but the victims themselves were removed before my arrival. I did not take any photographs myself. I wasn't the one using the camera. I don't know how many photos were taken or who took them, but it was a team from the security services centre who were performing this on-site investigation along with our team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that when you arrived there were no blood-marks or human bodies for that matter, were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. It was cleaned up the first time around. Most of it was cleaned up in the first go, so to speak, same as was the case at Markale. They tried to remove the bodies, but some blood-marks always remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At Markale, even those people who were killed were taken away immediately. Their bodies were removed; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a lot of cars, mostly Golf vehicles with their boots open. Bodies were placed inside, two or three bodies at a time, and they were taken away as soon as possible, or taken to the clinical centre if they were still to be treated. Those collecting the bodies were never entirely certain whether a body was dead or still alive. They just picked up the bodies as quickly as they could, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, can you confirm that at the time this occurred on the 18th of June, the school as such had not been operating in that building for a long time. There were no children there. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because right at the outset of the war, the aggressor bombed the school deliberately and used incendiary devices on the school. Not just this one, another school at Dobrinja as well. One was further to the west and the other was further to the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who removed the blood-marks so that we perhaps might be able to identify witnesses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I assume that, as is normally the case, it was the people who ran over to help, the people who took away the bodies. There someone -- there someone fetches some water and they try to clean up and remove the blood-marks. It's a perfectly normal, natural human reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, Official Note, which shows that you were involved --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can 65 ter document D13 please be shown. It's an official report. D13. I have to go back to that report, Your Honours, after what I've just heard. Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There, sir, the second-to-last paragraph, the previous one says: "The UNMOs were informed about the incident and they did not inspect the scene." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We said yesterday they came two hours later and they strongly objected about us doing anything. They said we were supposed to wait for them. If we'd waited for them all the time, we'd probably no longer be alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Next paragraph, and that's the reason I'm going back to this. You say: "The crime scene was secured by Sarajlija Hasan and Fuad Begic, members of the police." Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are police officers, members of the security services centre of Novi Grad, and they were the closest to the scene and they could secure it and inspect it. The Novi Grad police building was two buildings away from the actual crime scene, and this was part of Dobrinja, in purely administrative terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber how anyone at all was allowed to touch any evidence that was found at the site, such as blood-marks and the great number of people who were killed and injured there, since these people were securing the scene, as you say? Especially washing away the blood-marks - blood-marks, probably the single most important piece of evidence to be secured at any crime scene.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how to reply. There was a huge shock, human bodies blown to bits. Now to imagine that someone was to keep in mind things such as preserving evidence, not washing away the blood, keeping it just for all the world to see what we had been made to go through. Well, that spells a huge offence to the honour of the victims themselves. That's at least what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor refrained from showing photographs of any dead bodies yesterday in order to avoid causing shock. I think that was entirely justified. However, those photographs were taken at the morgue; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think the photographs were taken where the bodies were being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody clicked a camera; nobody took a single photograph at the actual site, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with the photographs. I didn't see anyone taking photographs. My job was a different one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that your team did the sort of job that is normally done in cases like these; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever investigators do at a crime scene is always an error. If they photograph dead bodies at a crime scene, they're accused of photographing dummies that were made to look like dead bodies. If the bodies were taken away, why were they taken away. If the blood-marks are washed away, why are they washed away. Why is there 12 litres of blood only? Why is there not only as much as -- as many as 5 litres. So what you're suggesting very much like sounds like causing offence to the honour of the dead victims to me, sir. Let me suggest that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was pursuing my line of work throughout the war. I was greatly affected by the sufferings of the people of that country. But you have to explain some things. Those investigating the crimes should do what is necessary so that now this Court could reach a judgement that would be reasonable and justified. That's all I am asking you about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I did. I can only speak on my behalf. I was highly professional in doing my job. We determined the equipment and the kind of weapon used in each of the incidents that we handled; the point of impact, the angle of descent. Whatever happened to be our job, we did it in a highly professional manner. As for this UNPROFOR report, it's not true that they removed any evidence. The wall that the shell hit remained there for years, completely intact. The next day, in 10 days, in 15 days, you could always go back and check where the shell had come from as well as the direction stated in the report. Whatever is in that report is just so, so, biased that I would be hard put to identify a single report that I've seen in my life that was less competent and more biased.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers kindly be reminded to observe a pause between questions an answers and also, please, to slow down for the benefit of the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will remind them. Did you hear that? The interpreter is asking you to slow down. You are speaking too fast and you're overlapping. You must observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I keep in mind the instructions received from His Honour Judge Mindua. I wait for the last letter on the screen to appear before I ask my question. So this time it's not my fault, thanks to the instructions previously received from His Honour Judge Mindua. If the witness is speaking fast, I think he is the one who should be cautioned and told to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, all of this happened on that spot on that same day. Was it not the case, in fact, that same day Sarajevo and the entire world watched a school get hit on their TV screens; people being killed, over 20 people being killed? Everybody knew. This piece of news was broken to everybody that a great crime had taken place and this was something that had been done by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Even on our TV it was said that the shell had arrived from Lukavica. It was not true. That was erroneous. That was an error made by the journalists. After the evening news, the next day, I went there again. I conducted an analysis again, once again to ascertain the facts. However, the news of this horrible crime went around the world, and rightly so, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can we please have a look at 65 ter 533. This is another UNPROFOR report in relation to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no B/C/S translation of this document. I would like to have page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have a translation and I will read it to you. Page 2, indeed. Do you see that witness? All right. You don't speak English, or do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's fine. I'm sure that we'll have no trouble understanding each other. Just cite the relevant portion and zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I have to translate this into B/C/S. But the passage marked as "A," halfway down the passage, the first word of the relative portion is "Total" Can you see that? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halfway through?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The sentence begins with the following words.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Sarajevo airport was opened shortly today ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Take the word "Total." There were a total of -- but you don't speak English, so that's why I am reading from the B/C/S copy. "There were also a total of 305 explosions." Can you see, sir? It reads: "There were also a total of 305 explosions reported." Can you see that? "Most in the areas of Igman, Butmir, Osijek airport, Ilidza, Nedzarici," and a number, "the 18th of June, 1995. A 120-millimetre mortar shell impacted in Dobrinja in an area where civilians were collecting water, killing seven civilians and wounding 11."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Has the witness found it? It's near the top. It's actually the second sentence in paragraph A, or the third sentence in paragraph A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it. "A 120-millimetre shell impacted in Dobrinja in an area where civilians were collected water. Seven civilians were killed ..." and so on and so forth. I see the sentence. "The Sarajevo airport was opened shortly today to allow a French soldier ..." I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I read that. Is that what it says? This is a report dated the 18th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all see that that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that true, what it says? That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm. I have no knowledge of that. I'm under oath. I can't just extemporise. I'm not sure if this many shells fell on these areas. I don't have accurate information indicating that and I simply can't say. Simple answer: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about this bit about the shell hitting the school at Dobrinja? You can confirm that, can't you? "... in an area where civilians were collecting water. Seven civilians were killed and 11 wounded." That's what the report says, and it's dated the 18th. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the date of the report. Perhaps it's somewhere at the top of the page. If everybody else can see it, then that's all right, I suppose. That's what it says, but that's as far as I can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 1 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can that please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see the date is the 18th; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "2359B, June 95." Is that it? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very weird method of writing down a date. "182395BJUN95," never seen a thing like that in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You can't say whether it's the 18th of June, can you? And you do speak English, or at least that's what you claim.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never before set eyes on this document. It says page 201 in the upper right corner, and then the 19th of June, 1995. That's what it says, not the 18th, in the upper right corner of the page. There, right there, the bit that is zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you look further down the page, there's talk of the 18th there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it says, "Date: 182359B June 95." It's a code that they used. I can't comment on it. I have never seen a date written down like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to waste any more time. I need your assistance here. I don't know how to proceed in this situation. The witness disagrees in a certain way that this is the 18th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think he disagrees. He just says that he is not familiar with that way of writing the date. But what is the question that you want to put to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First, the UNPROFOR report that I showed you yesterday, dated the 19th, you completely disagree with it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was totally incompetent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This report was dated the 18th, before the UNPROFOR report that you disagree with was prepared. Now, what I would like to present to you is on pages 6 and 7 of this report that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it, where it says "UNPROFOR ..." first, second, third, fourth, fifth -- please look at paragraph 6, and I'm going to read it out to you. "Bosnian media reported that as many as nine civilians were killed and 16 were injured in the Dobrinja area when two BSA shells impacted where they had gathered to collect water. UNMOs were able to confirm that seven were killed in the incident and were informed that there were ten wounded. (UNMOs are still unable to have free access to hospitals given present BiH restrictions). In reaction to the shelling, Bosnian Prime Minister Silajdzic reportedly stated his intention to once again press to have the armed embargo lifted." Is that what it says here? And can you confirm what we just said a while ago that the Bosnian media took this course of action and that Silajdzic made this statement publicly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment I don't know anything about this kind of statement given by Mr. Silajdzic, but I do know that he repeatedly said that the arms embargo should be lifted from Bosnia-Herzegovina, the arms embargo, that is, because we were the only ones subjected to these embargoes. For four years we were disarmed an attacked. By this, he wanted to emphasise the right to self-defence, which is a primary right which overrides all other rights. Every tree has a right to defend itself from insect. Every animal has a right to self-defence. Why shouldn't a human being have it? That is as far as self-defence is concerned. Concerning the media, they often portray distorted pictures. I told you that on the news that night it was said that the shell had come from Lukavica, that is, from the west, and that was wrong information. The shell had come from the east -- I apologise, from north-west, and the UNPROFOR report that you refer to denies itself in the sentence where it says that the shell had probably come from the west or from north-west. This kind of ambiguity is totally unacceptable when it comes to a serious UNMO officer's report. For that reason, I don't take this report to be a relative piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At this point in time, after everything you said about the direction from which the shell had come, I'm not going to ask you any further questions. In my view, this should be done by somebody who had more expertise than you. But I would like to ask you and suggest to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just proceed to do your job. Leave out the comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And my suggestion is that there were no seven people killed in this incident, nor 20, as originally reported, injured people, as it is stated in the report. I put it to you that this is not true, and I would kindly ask you to tell me what you think about this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a saying in Bosnia about this war which says that all shells that did not kill or wound anyone were fired by the Serbs. All the shells that killed people and maimed people were fired by the Bosnians. This is a paradox and this was part of the crime and part of the pattern of this war of intimidation. However, all the denials relating to victims I personally deeply feel as being offensive and something that kills these people for the second time. I deeply believe in that, and I'm very sorry that we didn't see these photographs yesterday, because that was something that occurred on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In future, I want shorter answers from you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm the fact that the photographs were taken in the morgue rather than on the scene where they were allegedly killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you for the sixth time that I know nothing about who took the photographs, what was photographed, et cetera. I had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that the Prosecutor was wrong yesterday for suggesting that we do not look at these photographs from the morgue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we would have grasped the situation better and understood what actually happened had we emotionally travelled back in time and seen these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, after all this, these casualties were presented and portrayed in the world as victims of the Serb shells; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I move that 65 ter 533 be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D74, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A respectable officer of NATO, General Nicolai, has been examined here in this courtroom and, according to the transcript, page 1004, line 13, he confirmed the following, and I'm going read it out to you. It read as follows: "One of the examples of the attitude taken by the Bosnians was when Minister Muratovic complained about the sniping of the water distribution point and requested protection from the UN. When I asked him where this point was, my interpreter explained to me that it was on the Square of Heroes, near the confrontation line, and it is completely visible to the VRS. I said to Muratovic that in that way sniper activities could be provoked, and suggested to him that this point be moved to a safer location." Now, my question to you is: Did you know about these tactics pursued by your minister, because at the time you were employed with the Ministry of the Interior, which was conducive to provoking sniper activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the interruption, but I've been notified by the AV booth again that counsel's microphone is not being turned off on a regular basis. It might also be helpful to suggest to the witness that he not speak if he sees that the red light of counsel's microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you must turn your mic off when you're not speaking because the witness is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has everything that I've said been recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So can you confirm that your superior pursued these kind of tactics and that he had been first warned about it by UNPROFOR and then -- do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is a very cynical interpretation of the situation in which civilians, by the very fact they existed and needed water to survive, irritated sharp-shooters. What were the snipers doing there? They were just sitting there and shooting randomly at densely populated places, and 90 per cent of the civilians were killed by them. I was wounded by a sniper to my leg. Luckily there were no serious consequences. And that was the place where the sharp-shooter was active all the time in order to sever Dobrinja from the rest of Sarajevo. Whatever was moving, an old man, a woman, a child, was the target. Anyone showing any signs of life --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you straightforwardly, did the BiH army fire from such positions as to provoke the activity of the VRS that was obliged to protect their men and fighters? There were civilians there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't know how the witness is able to answer that. He was not in the military; he was in the police during the time of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us hear his answer. Short answer. What's your answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can answer. It was technically impossible for Minister Muratovic to say or determine how water was to be fetched and how the people should behave there. Had he given such an order, nobody would have folded. So these collection points were part of their right to life, and even that was being -- tried to be taken away from people in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, just try to answer the question as straightforwardly as possible. The question was: Did the BiH army fire from such positions to provoke the activity of the VRS? And what is the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all. It was impossible. That's an insane idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, on that day were this fierce fighting from both sides during this offensive in those days? We are talking about the 18th of June. Was there intense activity on both sides, on both warring sides, that they were firing from heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that because I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to present something to the witness, but I'm aware of the time constraints.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about air bombs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to go back to what you said yesterday, but every time the victims of these bombs were mentioned a position was immediately taken and it was spread all over the world that these bombs killed many people and inflicted huge damage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When they hit the densely populated area, that was true. But sometimes they fell in fields and other unpopulated areas, creating only a huge crater there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put to you again the statement given by the witness I mentioned yesterday. His name was Hansen and he was supposed to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's DD00- --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's D72.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 3. I think it's page 3 in both versions. Please look at the third paragraph from the bottom, which reads: "An UNMO informed me that he had seen the shelling of the TV building." That's the incident of the 28th of June, 1995. Do you remember that incident where the TV building was hit by a shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the incident described in this way, but we are talking again about the report that I commented on. This is not a report compiled in proper military language. This is like hearsay or rumours; this person said this and that person said that. In the way, how it's written, its style and its arguments, this report, unfortunately, does not merit any attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You are protesting even before I read anything to you. Let me go on. I don't know how you know what I'm going to read.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "This shell that hit the TV building was fired by the BiH army." What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat again: This report does not resemble any proper military report or expertise. This is like old wives sitting around and having coffee and commenting on the incidents. This is my general view about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness please give me shorter answers. I am just putting to him what is written in this report. I didn't even ask him a question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have already asked him to give short answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at what it says onwards. "Another UNMO who heard the bomb told me that the bomb only flew for a short period which fitted with the findings of the first UNMO that the bomb was fired from BiH-held territory. I sent my report about this event to my superiors by secure means." My question is: You know that the BH army or, before that, the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina had at their disposal these kinds of air bombs, and that in this particular instance, a group of MUP members launched this bomb at the TV building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There are two questions there. The first question is: Do you know that the BH army or, before that, the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina had at their disposal these kinds of air bombs? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we definitely didn't have these kind of air bombs. But the question was put to me with the underlying claim that I know anything about this, and I'm saying that this is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The second part of the question was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The second part of the question was that in this particular instance, a group of MUP members launched this bomb at the TV building. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday, in response to the Prosecutor's questions, you said that when investigating these kind of events, no one had such experience anywhere in the world as you and your team had when it comes to these kind of incidents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. There is no information, historical information, that any city had been under siege for such a long time and been shelled, so that's our experience. And also military surgeons had enormous experience working in Sarajevo because there were wounded people coming in on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I never questioned or doubted medical conscience, and I know that the doctors in Sarajevo were very busy. I never doubted that. I questioned here a few very young people who were part of your teams, among others, an 18-year-old boy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I object, because when counsel is talking about part of his team, he has to be more specific. The witness's team is the KDZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, there's merit in that. The 18-year-old boy was not a part of his team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He already confirmed that there were young members of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I can ask him if there was any young person in his team.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were young people, but at the time they were all over 18 years of age. I repeat again: There were young people, but there were no 18-year-olds or under-18-year-olds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand now. First you said that there were young people. Now you denied it. What is the truth, the first thing or the second thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question was not clear. You said that you had questioned an 18-year-old man. If you questioned him here, then he must have been 8 years old during the war, so that's not clear to me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was not very precise. At the time, during the war when he was working there, he was 18, when he was a member of the investigation team.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about such person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, in my submission, the witness' answer is very clear. He has said there were no 18-year-olds or under-18-year-olds on his team. That leaves open the possibility there was a 19-year-old, I admit. But the question, in my view, has been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not allowed to comment on this, but let me ask you this: I'm asking you, at the time when the war broke out, what did you know at all about weapons, given that you were an expert in a certain field? What did you know about weapons that existed at the time in the world in various armies, including the JNA, including the BH army and the VRS army? What did you know about those kinds of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our army learned so much during the war that they became much more versed in weapons than some of the professionals. Those who have to defend themselves learn very fast about weapons, how they operate, et cetera, and the level is very quickly reached. What I knew before that, my father was a hunter. As a child I read a lot about it and probably I knew quite a lot about the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about hunting weapons. I'm asking you about heavy weaponry, about serious things that every army in the world used. What did you know at all about how certain weapons operate under certain circumstances? Did you have any basic knowledge; and if you did, where did you acquire it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew nothing about heavy weapons but you saw the math involved in calculating the angle of descent. That's secondary school level mathematics. That's when trigonometry is taught. It's basic maths, you might say. You can find the same thing in the textbooks used in the JNA for operating mortars, how exactly it works. This sort of knowledge is acquired in a perfectly simple way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll take your word for it, but let me ask you this: Why did none of your teams ever include any top-qualified military experts who know about each and every weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such military experts to be used. Wherever there were any, they were at the front line where their presence was badly needed to protect their people. Some of them in Sarajevo were experts for military production and they were always available to our investigation units to consult in order to resolve any problems that we came across.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm putting it to you that they refused to accept your methods, the methods that you, the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP, used in your work; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me that, I have to say I disagree. They were at the front lines where their presence was most needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the reports that we've gone through involving you? I never found a single opinion by an investigating magistrate. How do you explain that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had magistrates running or being in charge of many of these investigations, but in -- many times it was the case that an investigating magistrate simply could not physically be in charge of everything. Many of these reports begin by the following wording, "The Investigating Magistrate such-and-such conducted an analysis to the extent that ..." However, in Sarajevo, we would have needed to have thousands and thousands of investigating magistrates for them to be in charge of everything. This was war, not peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the incidents that you investigated. There is not a single opinion proffered there by an investigating magistrate; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know that in many of the cases, Zdenko Eterovic, who for a while was an investigating magistrate in Sarajevo, would join us quite a number of times on our way to a crime scene, and the team would, as a rule, be coordinated by this investigating magistrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you precisely about the incidents that you investigated, the Simone Bolivar school, the Markale incident and some other incidents. Why no opinions there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that. It wasn't down to me whether an investigating magistrate would be present or not. I think there were opinions offered by those and I think there must be other documents that reflect the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke many times yesterday about the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina was under the protection of the United Nations. Do you know about any country that is under the protection of the United Nations where investigations are conducted without the expertise of investigating magistrates? I'm talking about any country that is under UN protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object because the witness is only going to have to speculate on this. How is he to know what are the internal workings of the legal systems in other countries under UN mandate? What's the basis of his knowledge for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let him say. Do you know any knowledge of this? Short answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it this way: Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised by the UN, but it was left to its own devices in a way that no country had ever been. It was left to do or die.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next question. This is not getting us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there can be no legal system without courts. That lies at the heart of my question. I have received my answer. It is not my intention to dwell on this. However, DD00-0843, that is the document that I intend to show now. These are the proofing notes for Witness 137 by Mr. Sachdeva on the 14th of February, 2007. These notes have been translated. DD00-0843.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I just, Mr. President, ensure that this is not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Court Deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I've informed the AV booth not to broadcast it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can't see the witness's name anywhere. These are notes that I received from Mr. Sachdeva. This was produced on the 14th of February; that's the one I'm talking about. The Prosecutor should have the document. Nevertheless, can I please be allowed to question the witness on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like for the Chamber to have the document in front of it. 847. It's not 843; it's 847.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that the document on the screen now? Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see that, sir, don't you? You talked to the Prosecutor on the 14th of February, to Mr. Sachdeva; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here is what the first sentence says: "With respect to possible bias within the French UNPROFOR troops, the witness related a story regarding a massacre in 1994 in which two children were killed." Is that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR conducted their investigation whilst the witness and his team conducted theirs." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "The UNPROFOR report stated that there was shelling from Serb and BH positions." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "The Serb shelling did not injure anyone whilst the BH shelling was responsible for the casualties." Wasn't that what the UNPROFOR report said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the UNPROFOR report said, and thank you very much for asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "There was this agreement as to the distance which the shell would have travelled. The witness states that he spoke to two French UNPROFOR soldiers who were using a Vietnamese range table which had insignia from the Vietnam war. This table was based on 82-millimetre mortars with different parameters to the 82-millimetre mortars used in this incident. The Vietnamese table shows a much shorter firing range which would suggest the Bosnian government was firing on its own people. The actual mortars used had a much larger firing range." My question, sir: The French soldiers were wrong and you were right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The French soldiers were, as I believe, deliberately wrong in order to present evidence in an erroneous light and to mislead everyone. The thing is, both mortars had the same calibre; however, all they had to go on were two poor photocopies to determine the firing range. The entire range turned out to be much shorter as opposed to the weapon that was used in this area. It's, for example, as if you had a Volkswagen car and you were using a maintenance book for a Citroen car. The thing is, the table of ranges showed totally erroneous values and did not correspond with the weapon that was used in the area. This is one of the many cases where the French UNPROFOR soldiers provided erroneous information. Even when their own soldier was hit by sniper, they wouldn't allow the case to be investigated, nor did they submit his shirt for analysis, which would have proven beyond any doubt at all that he had been killed by a shot that had been fired from positions held by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, would the French soldiers, being members of one of the most honourable armies in world history --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I stopped you because the interpreter was having a very difficult time. You started your question before the interpretation was concluded. So just let us have the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, would the French soldiers, being members of one of the most honourable armies in the history of civilisation let themselves down, counteract what their own conscience would tell them to do and do something different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only they can say. I'm a witness to the fact that they had tables that did not correspond, were not consistent, with the mortar weapon from which the shell was used. It's not that they were ignorant. They were told to do it that way. Who instructed them to do just that, I don't know. You should go and ask them. Only they can answer that question. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence of your interview with Mr. Sachdeva reads: "He suggested that this reflected a French policy bias towards the Serbs." Is that your position, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were, unfortunately, many cases in relation to which this was the only possible interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was tendered as D66 MFI, our Exhibit DD00-0681. Can I please have the Court's permission to show the witness the document? This is what the President of BH, Alija Izetbegovic, found out from the French ambassador.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to read the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And how long is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There. Have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I inquire if there's a translation available?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have a translation? If not, it's a relatively short document. Go ahead, read slowly, and we'll have the interpreters ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look, sir. Do you see that this is from the main logistics centre of the BH army? You see that; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see the following paragraph, Presidency of BH -- this is being sent to General Delic, the commander of the General Staff of the BH army. Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Further down: "General, just this morning, the French Ambassador Henri Zakolen visited my office and, among other things, shared this with my advisor Memija: France makes it official that it is furious over the murder of one of its soldiers at Dobrinja. Military expertise has shown that the soldier had been hit from a position held by the Bosnian army. We have not been allowed an inspection which gives rise to doubt and suspicion. The Chetniks have, in this particular incident, displayed an unlimited willingness to cooperate by allowing UN investigators to enter every flat in each and every position along their own line. Our men, on the other hand, have refused each form of cooperation by not allowing access to any of the numerous locations from which our soldier could have been hit." He said: "Once the BH army has allowed the UNPROFOR commission access to the buildings from which the bullet could have been fired at the French soldier, we shall be able to speak of a normalisation of relations between Paris and Sarajevo. The French ambassador caused us an unpleasant surprise by saying that he had evidence that over half of the 24 murders of their soldiers from the UN troops, not counting those killed in the traffic accident at Igman, were committed by the BH army." He goes on to say: "General Gobillard complained to him that for weeks our own commanders had been refusing contact with UNPROFOR." He went on to add: "We do not understand this kind of behaviour and we do not see what can possibly be achieved in this way. Of course, some of these statements should be taken with a pinch of salt, but it's also necessary for you to know what their objections are. Remove any obstacles to cooperation wherever these are not indispensable from a military point of view. Salam, Alija Izetbegovic, Sarajevo, 21 April 1995." Witness, in view of what you said about the French soldiers a while ago, the fact that you didn't trust them, in view of your belief that they had a pro-Serb bias, can we therefore say that this constituted a reason why French soldiers came under fire by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this report before. I have to repeat something that I was personally involved in and I can vouch for its truthfulness. Whatever this report says, it means nothing to me since I have never seen it before. I'm not involved in anything that concerns this report, and I can't testify to any allegations contained therein. I have to say again that I nearly clashed with them because they were using erroneous tables, indicating that we had been killing our own children, to all practical intents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question was a different one. Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Mr. Sachdeva wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no objection to this line of questioning. However, the specific question that counsel has asked, in my submission, asks the witness to put -- to be able to know what was in the mind of the BH army if and when they did fire upon French soldiers. I don't see how the witness can answer that, answer that specific question, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness has denied any knowledge of the document, so no questions should be put to him on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about his belief, the belief that existed that French UNPROFOR soldiers displayed a pro-Serb bias? Were those French soldiers ever targeted in the any action that involved any members of his own unit? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm deeply convinced that the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again I can't tender this document as a Defence exhibit. This remains D66 MFI, so I may have to reach for it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. Your line of questioning suggests that it would somehow be possible to identify French UNPROFOR soldiers from other UNPROFOR soldiers from a distance. So could you perhaps clarify with the witness whether, to his knowledge, it was possible to distinguish between a French UNPROFOR soldier and an UNPROFOR soldier from another country from a distance?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the trial proceeds, I may be able to show just that. During our defence case, I will also show how certain Serb citizens were picked out by BH snipers and how the snipers were informed about who the Serbs were in the streets of Sarajevo so that they could be targeted. I will prove that in my defence case. I think I will equally be able to prove by using other evidence - and we shall have French generals testify, and we'll hear something about that, too - that would have been a very easy thing to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel, I do not wish to interfere in any way with your line of questioning to the witness, but my suggestion was that you put to the witness the question of whether, to his knowledge, it was possible to distinguish French soldiers from other soldiers belonging to the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask the witness just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for one of the BH army members to inform someone further down the line in some way where the French soldiers were positioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about possibilities. Anything is possible. We need to ask ourselves who, where, when, but that doesn't prove anything in itself, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm happy with this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You haven't answered the question. Was it possible for the BH army or anyone else to distinguish between French UNPROFOR soldiers and others? Don't sermonise. Answer as directly as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All UNPROFOR soldiers look very much alike in terms of their general appearance. They each displayed the insignia of their own countries but very small ones. Only those who looked very high perhaps would have been able to distinguish, but to us they were all the same. It was that simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, next question. Well, we are -- one more question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have two or three topics that I would like to cover and I will try to wrap up as swiftly as I can after the break. I can't just ask a single question now before the break. I have this many documents to show, there, you see, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. At the accused's suggestion, I was instructed to ask one question of the witness and this concerns the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were certain members of certain armies deployed in specific areas, i.e., did they have specific areas that they controlled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question. I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: For instance, did the Russian Battalion cover a certain area? Did the French Battalion cover a certain area? Did the Ukrainian Battalion cover a certain area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot guarantee you that, but I think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any specific distinguishing marks? Not only patches, but they also had different helmets. They all wore uniforms of their representative armies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was obvious that there were different uniforms. Some had smaller patterns; some had bigger patterns.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Another question in this connection and it's a very important thing. Did you know that members of the police used to check -- ID people in the street, irrespective of their ethnicities, for security reasons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about these things happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about instances of IDs being checked, and once it was established that the person was a Serb, after 100 metres, a sniper would kill this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard speculations of that nature and even worse than that, but I don't believe that that was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there were three statements given by this witness, one given in 1995, et cetera, but it doesn't matter. I'm not going to ask him any questions relating to these statements, although there was an interesting one given on the 25th of November. I would move on now to an incident. It's P122, Prosecution Exhibit. If it can please be shown to the witness. That's an official report bearing the name of another protected witness, and if can we can go into private session before I ask him anything. Let's move to page 1 of this official report dated the 22nd of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 3 of this document, there's no name mentioned there, so in that respect this report, dated 22 June 1995, can be shown to witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, page 3, report on the forensic examination of the scene, can you see this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's rather unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have a perfectly clear copy in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have to say that what I'm seeing is not clear, that is, what is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've never received any better copy from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let's do our best with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it now. "Report on the shelling, Goethe Street Number 12, 22nd of June," and at the end it says: "Armedina Burik, a little girl, was killed." Is that what it says approximately here? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm this, that everything that is written here is completely accurate as far as you were involved in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think everything is in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to be very brief. Can you tell me how this girl was killed? You know that she was killed, according to this report, by an air bomb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that a wall had been penetrated, as stated by another protected witness, and that this girl was killed in a flat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that there was no penetration of the wall at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can kindly ask you not to tell me what it is that I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that is the way the question is put. He's putting to you that you know that, and if you don't know, then you say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were many such cases like this one. I believe that this was an incident in which this girl was in a pyjama in her house and that the father took her out already dead. The walls in this neighbourhood were made of soft concrete that even a bullet, a rifle bullet, can penetrate, let alone shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I asked you but what your team established on the spot. Your team established that the wall had been penetrated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this protected witness, whose name you just saw in the document, said here that this wall had not been penetrated at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what are you saying now? What are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm putting to you that this girl was not killed at this specific location at all. How long are we going to stare at each other?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why isn't he answering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know better about everything that happened, and you were never in Sarajevo at the time. You just don't believe us who were in Sarajevo. I don't know what you want me to answer you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He has put to you that the little girl was not killed at that specific location at all. What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember correctly, there were many cases. One cannot remember what you had for lunch three months ago, let alone cases like this. However, when we visited the scene, I remember that the girl's father took her out; he carried her in his arms. She was in pyjama. So what else do you want me to say? He carried her out, crying and screaming. Are we going to insult this man now by claiming that he had killed her?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since your team carried out the investigation, did you establish what happened in that flat? Did you photograph this punched wall and did you see any traces of the killing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself and my team didn't go to that flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No member of your team photographed the traces of this horrendous crime in this flat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to respond these kind of questions, I need to see the entire report. This is just a detail about the casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I received this document and other documents from the Prosecution. There is not a single photograph relating to what you just said. How do you account for the fact that there were no photographs taken in the room where this little girl was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no explanation for that. We didn't always carry a camera with us. My team almost never had a camera with us. This was to be done by the security services centre. We dealt with explosive charges and by establishing who was killed, who was wounded, and what damage was inflicted. Other forensic evidence was collected by the security services centre, and I believe that you will have an opportunity to ask them how they processed the scene, why they didn't take any photographs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not asking you about any case. I'm asking about this specific case presented here by the Prosecution and the investigation in which you took part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for raising late. However, I have had to check the transcript. And I just want to point out, just for clarity, that the protected witness that counsel has been talking about in fact said the following, if I may, with your leave. My question to the protected witness was this: "That damage to the facade that you speak of, was it caused by the projectile that exploded at the impact point that you've indicated with figure 1 on the sketch?" The answer was: "That's right. This damage was caused by a fragment of the projectile that tore through the wall and hit the little girl who was lying in her bed." In my submission, this is different to what counsel has put to the present witness, suggesting that -- suggesting that, and I quote his question, "and this protected witness, whose name you just saw in the document, said here that this wall had not been penetrated at all." I think that needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's correct. That's what he said in response to the Prosecutor's question. When he was presented with all this during cross-examination, he was asked to look carefully at the wall. I don't have it in front of me, but this part of the transcript, he said very decisively that after he had looked at the photograph carefully, the wall had not been penetrated. So the answer he gave to the Prosecutor is one thing; however, what he said during cross-examination is a different thing. And he did confirm, and he said it very firmly, that the wall had not been penetrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what portion of the transcript is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the portion of the cross-examination. I cannot look for it now - that is why I have curtailed my examination - but if it becomes necessary to explain this, I'm going to do that. So maybe if my -- if this question of mine is not being admitted, then I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what I'll do is I'll have the legal officer check the transcript and we can come back to that. But how much time -- how much more time are you planning to spend? You have now utilised the same amount of time, if not more, than the Prosecutor did in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree, but I will try to make it as brief as possible. I will not tackle these three statements that the witness gave. Let me now move on now to Markale, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you say you didn't agree? What didn't you agree with?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot be sure, Your Honour, because yesterday the Prosecutor took all three sessions yesterday and I only started my cross-examination during the last session. The Prosecutor took up two and a half sessions and that's what I remember. I started my cross-examination after ten past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll just check with the court deputy. Please go ahead. I'll ask the court deputy to give me the times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will stop the moment you tell me that I have exhausted my time, and rest assured that I will not object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we won't get into that now, but the court deputy said that the Prosecutor spent two hours and 24 minutes. He didn't count the 45 minutes of Judge's questions. We're not going to get into a discussion on time, because I'm not a time-keeper. And I really resent that I have to resort to a time-keeping exercise in a court of law, but it's a necessity. Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't intend to get into such discussion. I just want to -- for the benefit of the Court, the issue with respect to the wall and the penetration or not, my submission is answered by the protected witness that the counsel has identified on page -- it actually stems from a question from His Honour Judge Harhoff, 1389, 1390, 1391, those are the pages, and the date of the evidence is 1st of February, 2007, just for the benefit of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you spoke at length about Markale and the incident that happened there on the 28th of August, 1995. Can you tell me, first of all, from the place where the shell landed - and we're going to look at the photographs again - to Markale, there's more than 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we going to look at the photographs, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, but that's my first question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make it clear: There's a closed market and there's an open-air market at Markale. That was the same at Markale 1. So you are talking about the distance between the two? Is that what you are interested in?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you can specify the distance between the impact spot of the shell to either of the markets.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the case that we call Markale 1, the shell hit the open area. As for Markale 2, the distance between the closed market and this place, roughly speaking, is about 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not asking about Markale 1 at all. I'm asking you about the incident of the 28th of June, 1995, because that is the subject that is being discussed her.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What distance are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just so we clear up any confusion, the transcript has 28th of June - and that's what I heard in the interpretation - however, the Markale incident was on a different date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the date that you are putting to the witness, Mr. Tapuskovic, for the Markale incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is obviously a slip of the tongue. I'm not sure what I said. I was dealing with Markale 2, and that happened on the 28th of August, 1995. If anyone heard me saying "June," that could only have been a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So I'm asking the witness about the incident of the 28th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question. Which distance specifically are you interested in?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the distance between the place where the shell hit the pavement to Markale 1 open-air market and the other market, which is at a different place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll partly answer your question. The shell, first of all, did not land on the pavement but it landed on the driving lane. And the place where it landed, in the case of Markale 2, to the place where the shell landed in open-air market known as Markale 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
