utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I need your assistance. I'm not asking him about Markale 1 at all. I'm asking him about Markale 2, but the witness keeps mixing these two things and wasting our time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you are mixing the open-air market --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are being asked about Markale 2, the 28th of August, 1995. Would you answer the question as directly as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I will do my best, but I must remind the Chamber that Mr. Tapuskovic is mixing up the open-air market and the closed market, and that is probably why he is not putting the question rightly and therefore I cannot understand his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question was: What is the distance between the place where the shell hit the pavement to Markale 1 open-air market and the other market, which is at a different place? Was that the question, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just be very precise, if you'll allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You explained where the shell hit. Can you tell at which market were people killed by this shell on the 28th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the people who were in the street. Some were on motorcycles; some were pedestrians. And there was -- there's always a lot of people there as if it were a marketplace. They were all in the street in front of the gate to the closed market, which is the second most crowded selling point in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So they were killed in front of this closed-roofed market; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the people in the street. Yes, these people were in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In front of the market or on the street itself where the shell landed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly on the street in front of the market. But there's about 200 metres between the two markets, so there's always a large crowd of people, because that's the main market in Sarajevo where people come to do their shopping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the following photograph brought up, the first photograph: 65 ter number 2595, page 2, photograph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see that, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please show the spot in this photograph where the shell impacted. And mark it, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The image is not that clear, but I think this should be the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please use an arrow to indicate how the shrapnel spread.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bits closer to the pavement went down and the remaining shards flew in a circular motion and spread that way, roughly speaking. The direction is not right because it flew over the building. And if can I just make a small correction there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Explain the direction in relation to this roofed-over, closed market.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just in front. It's this building right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that there were over 150 people in this place, 120.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is if right now, as we speak, you called Sarajevo, told them to block the traffic and count all the people there, you would find about 100 people there between the spot where the shell landed and the open-air market, which is over here, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between this place and the open-air market?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 200 metres that I told you about, 200 metres in this direction, where the arrow points. Open-air market, "OM." The open-air market and the indoor market, the one over here, constituted the greatest concentration of shops with food in Sarajevo at the time. I went on a monthly basis here. I carried the cigarettes there, since I didn't smoke myself, and I exchanged those for food. A kilogramme of sugar was 100 German marks, and so on and so forth. This was a place that ensured survival. People exchanged goods there, and this was the greatest possible concentration of living human beings in an open area in the entire town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show the Chamber, what is the distance between the place where the shell landed and impacted and the corner of this building here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this car, behind this car? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question was clear, wasn't it? The place where the shell impacted against the ground and the corner of this yellow building to the right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the one you mean? Here, I'm marking it for you. Maybe some 7 metres, but that's just a very rough estimate based on me looking at this photograph. It's nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, at 11.15 you had used two hours and 34 minutes, ten minutes more than the examination-in-chief. We will give you until 12.00 noon to conclude the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be sure to finish by then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I wasn't asking you about that corner. I'm asking you about the corner up front here which can't be seen because of the car that's parked there. The yellow building, what is that distance? You keep doing something that is not what I'm asking you to do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're saying things the other way around. I asked you about the corner behind the car and you said no. I said the corner behind the car? You said no, so I drew the other one. So you must be asking me about this corner. 8 metres, perhaps, 13 years later, but based on a memory that isn't as clear as it used to be. It could be anything between 6 and 8 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is crystal clear. I said the building behind the car, not the corner. I wasn't asking you about that. I'm asking about the distance between the place the shell hit the building behind the car, its corner. That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building has two corners. This is one of the corners, the blue dot, and the other one is behind the car. I can't see the other corner. Which one do you mean? There are two on the southern side of the building and four more up on the roof. So, please, can you try to be a bit more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't possibly be more specific, Witness. I'm asking about the distance between the impact of the shell and the dot you drew on the car. What's the distance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 6 metres, 8 metres, perhaps. Nobody knows the respective distances with the possible exception of the architects who built the building and maybe dwelled on these specific distances. My shot would be between 6 and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go into closed -- private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe you indicated when we were in private session that you wanted to have this admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another moment, Your Honour. I would like to ask something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Honourable Witness, you say it was possible for a shell to be timed in such a way as to impact between these two buildings, each about 4 or 5 metres long, and land exactly in the spot where it landed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that shells are even more accurate than that. And if you have an artillery expert, they will tell you that he can hit a kitchen plate at quite some distance or target the opening of a chimney. That's how they describe the accuracy of a shell. Hitting a street that's at least 8 metres across is no great deal at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm very upset at what you did. Let us go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D75, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Esteemed Witness, you said yesterday that you'd only heard a single explosion. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were five explosions in this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How come you were there ten minutes later and not in any of the other four locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was off with one of my colleagues from the bomb squad to this particular location, and then on the main street, 200 metres to the west, I saw a huge number of cars sounding their horns, with human arms and legs sticking out of the cars. We knew that something horrible had happened. We went back to the bomb squad unit, which was three or four minutes from there. We collected our equipment and went back to this same place, which took about seven or eight minutes altogether. The respective distances are several hundred metres in each case. The bomb squad headquarters was near the central bank office of Sarajevo, the national bank with the statues and everything. If you walk fast, it takes about seven or eight minutes. I was halfway there not when the shell landed, but rather, I with my colleague, we had been off to the market to exchange some cigarettes for some food coupons. I saw a large number of cars and deafening noise of the horns being sounded, carrying bodies of dead and wounded people, arms and legs sticking out of the boots of those cars, blood all over the place, taking them to Kosevo. We were there in no time at all because that was our place, that was our headquarters. It was God's will that I wasn't there myself five or ten minutes earlier, because had I been there five or ten minutes earlier, I would have come to grief as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know about Markale 1, right, the 5th of February, 1994? A single shell was fired which led the experts to doubt the accuracy of the targeting, how it was possible to target so accurately with a single shell. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, but I'm deeply convinced that NATO experts will tell you that was no problem at all. If you had a mortar position and emplacement, if it had been there for a long time, they would have had the coordinates, they would have had all the necessary parameters, and they would have been perfectly able to target any grid reference in Sarajevo with a very high degree of accuracy. Besides, their positions were high up in the mountains surrounding the town, and that would have made it even easier for them to target specific locations inside the town, because Sarajevo was virtually in the palm of their hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The town was in some sort of a valley, a hole; I know that. But the claim here is that this came from Trebevic. Colina Kapa is part of Trebevic, yet it's 1.000 metres high. In theory, the shell could have come from Trebevic, couldn't it? From Colina Kapa; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came from an azimuth that we determined, and I still stand by that assessment. The direction was determined with great accuracy. Even the UNPROFOR artillery men determined the same identical angle in relation to that shell that landed right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I'm putting it to you that at least five shells should have landed in order for you to be able to claim with certainty that what happened was a result of something that the army of Republika Srpska had done. And then there would no objections being raised about the possible accuracy of a single round being fired.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the forces of Republika Srpska were very experienced and they were extremely good at targeting what they wanted to target. I'm sure that this dilemma can be clarified by the Chamber if NATO artillery experts are brought in to confirm the incredible accuracy of angles of descent in case of shells. It is not used for horizontal targeting, as guns usually are. A shell is a weapon that is used for vertical targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You did not hear the sound of these five incoming shells, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that at the time the radar equipment was very poor, right, the radar equipment that was used.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. What I said was that the radars brought into Sarajevo by the French forces at the beginning of the war, promising that each projectile fired would be photographed in the air indicating the direction and source of firing, so this radar, five days later, was declared officially to be out of working order. Obviously, any information produced by that radar was later used for just filing away, but it certainly wasn't used for any other more helpful purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A well-regarded expert on weapons, radars, and other types of technology testified before this Court, General Nicolai. At page 1023 through 1024, General Nicolai spoke about the fact that at the time of this incident - I have to do this the way the Prosecutor thinks I should, and it's the normal way to do it - General Nicolai stated that at the time of this incident, which occurred on the 28th of August, 1995, there was a cutting-edge Dutch device for monitoring what was going on in the Sarajevo area. Likewise, the English Battalion had very up-to-date radar technology to monitor the Sarajevo area. He said that those radars had registered nothing at all, no shell flying, and not even those five shells fired allegedly from territory under the control of the BH army -- I mean the army of Republika Srpska, or the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina for that matter. My question is: Why is it that you're saying that there was no -- there were no radars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not my duty to know what sort of equipment different sections of UNPROFOR are using. That would probably be confidential information anyway. Report G2, all right, I see what the source is of this security. I see that there no radar -- artillery activity from positions held by the BH army on the day in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I really want to know is nothing was registered as being fired from the area under the control of the Republika Srpska army. The radars never clocked anything. How can you explain that? How can you explain the fact that the radars would never clock a thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm facing a very unpleasant situation here. It seems that there were no dead. It seems the whole war was not real. It was just a very bad nightmare. The radars didn't catch it; therefore, we just dreamt it. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next question. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. People did die; people were killed; lives were lost on both sides. But what I'm talking about here - that's what I'm putting to you - is these were explosions that were planted and activated by telecommand, teleactivated, and there were no victims at all when these explosions occurred. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the blackest lie I have ever heard in my life. This is the third time these same victims get killed. The first time, they're physically killed; the second time around, they are denied; the third time around, this is made a laughing matter on TV where the victims are mocked. So all this achieves is an endless mockery of Sarajevo's victims, which included over 1.500 children under 12 years of age, and go figure what the rest of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There were both Serbs and Croats among the victims, as well as Muslims; would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that many Serbs stayed back in Sarajevo. Many of them joined the ranks of the BH army. As for my own bomb squad unit, there were more Croats and Serbs than Bosniaks. They were all loyal citizens, honourable citizens, who tried to get on with their lives. But an exploding shell does not distinguish along ethnic lines. Those up on the hills who were targeting everybody else took everybody else down in the valley to be their enemy. So they just killed indiscriminately. That's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that, don't I? But there's this one shell that I'm talking about all the time. This shell killed members of all the different ethnicities living in the former Yugoslavia indiscriminately, didn't it, including Muslims, Serbs, Croats. The victims of this shelling included all the different ethnicities, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think the names of the victims that I saw at the time included Serb and Croat names as well, so it seems that you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at P250.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you rule out the possibility that the shell hit the roof?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You do, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, because people went up to the roof in order to be high up and look down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Had it hit the roof, the shrapnel would have spread wide; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had it hit the roof, no one would have been killed, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Explain, please. I see a lot of blood here. It's not a joyous sight exactly. The shell hit right here, it impacted right here. How is it possible that those two bikes leaning against the wall are not blood-spattered? Not a single spot of blood, and the bikes are still there, standing upright. How can you possibly explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a perfectly simple and logical explanation. Those bikes were being used elsewhere at the time. When the road was cleared of the dead bodies and the injured, the two things that were found in the way, obviously, these two bikes, were pushed aside so that they weren't in the way of passing traffic. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The President, Judge Robinson, asked you about that. So the traffic just got on with it and the bikes were there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay any attention to the bikes at all, but what I'm saying now is what I think to be the most probable thing. They were probably taken onto the pavement in order for them not to be in the way. But UNPROFOR forces arrived, other cars arrived; ambulances had been called. The road had to be open. If you have a bike lying upside down in the middle of the road, this is normally something that you need to remove in order to make sure that the traffic flow remains unhindered. On the right-hand wheel of this bicycle, you can see a lot of blood. If you zoom in on it, you can see there's a lot of blood there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I won't go back to this because I have very little time left. This is a self-explanatory photograph. Answer me this: If there were thousands of shrapnel pieces produced by this shell -- tell me first, do you know, how much does this shell way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, around 12 kilos altogether. I think there is about 2.5 kilos of TNT inside it, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's the weight of the shell, and it produced mass shrapnel. Were there any shrapnel hitting the walls of these buildings, since so many people were killed? And can we see on any photograph that can -- the Prosecution can provide showing traces of shrapnel on the wall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely clearly remember there were lots of damaged places in the walls of the buildings. And we also examined the distribution of this damage, because you can see that most of the shrapnel fell on the pavement and on the opposite side, to the north. The damage was a few metres high up from the ground on the windows and the walls, which confirms our theory about the geometry of the dispersion of shrapnel. So there is a lot of damage visible on the buildings surrounding this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My last question about Markale in order to make it possible for me to put some more questions to you. Some other witnesses are going to testify about this. I do understand that over 80 wounded people were removed from the location immediately, and this is something that must be done. But for the sake and the truth of investigation, was it not required for these wounded people -- or for the people who were killed, why were they so hastily removed from the location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this instance as well as in other instances, civilians run there to offer help, who were on the shot, or the passers-by and the cars. All these people were laymen. If people don't show any signs of life, it does not mean necessarily that they were dead. However, people passing by tried to help. Cars stop. They packed the people inside without thinking about it, took them to the hospital. They just followed their instinct, their human instinct to bring those people to hospital where possibly - and laymen cannot say that - these people can be given help and assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry that the Prosecution didn't show the photographs of these people. It was evident for at least 10 or 15 people that they were already dead. You went there as experts and you were supposed to provide conclusive evidence about everything. Why did you permit the people who were definitely dead to be removed from the site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reminding you that I said that some 200 metres from that place, I was headed for the market and I saw for myself already a large number of cars driving people there. There was no police there, no authorities, no officials. People were just taking away the casualties. That's what I saw. I went back to our HQ and then I returned there. Everything that was done there was done spontaneously. Keeping the dead on the spot in order to do the measurements, to measure how much blood is required, how many litres of blood -- how much do you need, 200 litres? Thirty people times 5 litres of blood, that makes 150 litres of blood, and that's only from the dead. I am not counting the blood from the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I still put it to you to that they were not killed in this place. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely untrue. In the wide area, pieces of brain, of skulls, of fingers, were found. The shrapnel travelled downwards from this place and they severed off people's feet completely. And there was so much of that stuff there that had this been planted, it would have been noticed by hundreds of witnesses. So both theoretically and practically it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, can I ask you, is it your allegation that the blood we see on the frame here was not coming out of the victims of the shell but was put there deliberately by someone else afterwards; is that your allegation? And do you have any foundation for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm suggesting with full responsibility, not only for Defence counsel for Dragomir Milosevic, that at this location of the explosion there were no casualties at all; that those who were killed were absolutely killed elsewhere and then brought to the location and quickly removed again in order to preclude any proper investigation there. This is what I'm claiming, and I stand behind this, and I believe that these proceedings are going to demonstrate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But could you help the Chamber to lay some foundation for this allegation? What is the evidence that you are relying upon in putting this to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A series of evidence that has already been presented, including the fact that the flight of this projectile had not been registered. Also, there was no sound registered of the shell flying and a series of other things that will later be established. But primarily, there is no fact to support that these shells landed where they exploded, but that they were rather explosive devices planted at the time when there were no casualties in other locations and then these casualties were brought to this location. And this was proven in other incidents as well. This is why I left Markale for the end. The same happened in the case of Simone Bolivar school; the same happened with this little girl who was never killed in this place. So it's based on this evidence, and that's why I left Markale for the end, to question this witness about. But I believe that other events will show this, and this is the basis for my argument and for my putting this claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since the time is almost up, if I may just present one more document to the witness and thereby conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday the witness said that a million shells landed in Sarajevo and other projectiles as well. Is that correct, Witness? Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard many times this estimate. This estimate was made by a military expert who monitored the activities on a yearly basis, and that includes all kinds of projectiles, not only mortar shells. In this case, Your Honours, there are lots of survivors, thank God, who can verify and describe to you the situation and each and every incident that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me show to the witness, although I have about a dozen other documents. But I have one piece of evidence provided from the archive of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It refers to July 1995 and the consumption of, as they call it, "MTS" that is, ammunition, for the month of July. It's DD00-0733. It's not been translated yet. It refers to the consumption of the ammunition used and spent by the BH army in July 1995. DD00-0733.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that this is a report pertaining to July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Look at it towards the end, which speaks about the consumption of MTS.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Someone is scrolling it down. I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "July, consumption of MTS, 287.831 rounds of bullets," and then again "7.62 rounds of bullets," 16.000 and something. Then further on, "Shells, 60-millimetre shells, 82-millimetre shells." A total of around 500.000 mortar solely in July. I have no time to add these figures up, but at first glance you can see that in July the BH army fired at the positions of the VRS army this amount of various calibre ammunition. What can you say to that? Did you notice that there was so much firing in July at the Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that this report that we're all looking at on our screens is construed totally wrong. You said 500.000 shells. This huge number refers to bullets. And there is a very small number of shells. The comparison would be the same as if a fisherman caught a whale or a million of sardines. This refers to shells and rounds of all calibres. That includes only heavy artillery weapons. However, the ordinary bullets cannot be added to this total figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here, it says "TRM." What does that stand for? "3.230 pieces." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a tromblon mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then later on, "MB98, 201.850."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this D2 is. "P/GD2," I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no such thing as MB98.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My last question is: What's the range of the tromblon mine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's launched from a rifle, and at best it can reach a couple of hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With this I conclude my cross-examination. Can we please have this document DD00-0733 tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D76, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry. With your leave, Mr. President, could I leave the courtroom for just a few minutes before the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President. Can I ask that P255 be brought up, and if it could not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, this is a document that I showed to you in my examination-in-chief. Can you just remind the Court what this document is, please. And there should be an English translation as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this refers to the case of Markale, 28th of August, 11.30. Yes. I think that's an authentic document referring to the Markale case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have the English translation on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could be given the page reference, it would help greatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 137, if you go to the name that is listed, the first name, do you see the name Asim Kanlic there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asim?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Right, the first name there, Asim Kanlic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Court what -- next to the name there is something there which reflects his job description. What is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-137 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asim Kanlic is a judge of the high court in Sarajevo, and immediately after him, in order to anticipate your question, we have the prosecutor of the high public prosecutor's office in Sarajevo; therefore, we have legitimate officials here present directing the whole investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you'll allow me to say a few words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not the practice. I think you should just leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next witness. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be taking the next witness. If I may suggest, I had asked leave to present an oral motion concerning protective measures in between the two witnesses. May I suggest that we take that up and also one other motion that I have reason to believe that is uncontested, and then break so that we can make -- I think it will go far more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, yesterday in an e-mail, the -- first of all, could we go into private session--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, the witness testifies with the protective measure of facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Sir, could you begin by telling us your name and what you do for a living, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: My name is Sead Besic and I am a forensic technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Forensic technician. For whom do you work?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I work for the Sarajevo canton, Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is that a law enforcement or police agency?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are you a police officer?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How long have you been a police officer?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I have been with the police since 1975. I have been in the forensics department since 1987. I took a six-month training course to become a forensic officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber, please, in general, what the duties are of a forensic officer with the Sarajevo canton of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: We go to crime scenes. We take photographs. We video the crime scene, we film it. We collect evidence and submit any evidence found for analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you attend the scene of a shelling in the Markale market in Sarajevo on the 28th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you go there by yourself or did you go there as a member of a team?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I was with an on-site investigation team made up of a prosecutor, investigating judge, operatives and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you say "operatives," could you explain what that term means, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: These are operatives, operative officers, from the crime squad. They draw up a record at the scene, they take witness statements, and they monitor the whole process.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How was it that you and your team went to Markale market on the 28th of August, 1995? What were you responding to by going to the market?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: We received word at about 11.00 that a mortar shell had landed outside the entrance to Markale. We were supposed to conduct an on-site investigation. A team was put together, and about 15 or 30 minutes later, we arrived at the scene. This is the sort of thing that is usually done by the cantonal MUP, which was the CSB, the security services centre, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you arrived at the scene of the shelling in Markale market, did you observe any measures having been taken to preserve the integrity of the crime scene; and if the answer to that is yes, could you describe those measures to the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. The crime scene was secured by police officers from Centar municipality. Once they had arrived they did not allow anyone else near the crime scene until the on-site investigation team eventually arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you obtain any information as to what, if anything, had been done within the crime scene before you and the rest of your team arrived at Markale market on August 28th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that there had been quite a large number of dead and wounded and that the casualties had been taken to a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Within the team on that day, 28th of August, what were your specific duties? What was your role on that team on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: We were supposed to investigate the crime scene by taking photographs, by filming the scene, by making a sketch, and by collecting any evidence in relation to the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You received word at about 11.00 that a mortar shell had landed, and it took you about 15 to 30 minutes to get to the market. Were you able to find out more precisely when the mortar shell actually landed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The report came at about 11.00 or five past 11.00. It took us 30 minutes after that to set up a team, including a prosecutor, a judge and some operatives. The place where our station was was about 800 metres away from the scene of the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you in a position to say whether you received the report immediately after the incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The report reached the security services centre via a radio set and that's how we received the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'm trying to find out is whether you're in a position to say if any time elapsed between the shelling and the sending of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received the report after the shell had landed, after the shell had landed. We received the report at five past 11.00, possibly ten past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But how long after the shell landed did you receive the report, or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Officer, did you take photographs at the Markale market on the 28th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, have you taken the time to review the photographs that you took that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And are those photographs fair and accurate photographs of what you saw at the Markale market on that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the photographs have 65 ter number 00129. I'm not -- there are approximately 44 photographs in that ter number. I'm not going to take the witness through all of them, but I am going to ask that all 44 be admitted into evidence so that they are available, if needed. As a single -- as a single exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you going to show us at least one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to show you many more than one, Mr. President, but I'm not going show you all 44. And I also want to just put on the record that some of these 44 are of a disturbing nature and I'm not going to display those in court. If we could please have e-court page 1 of 65 ter number 00129 displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: While we wait for that, Officer -- oh, never mind. Is this one of the photographs that you took that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And can you tell us the name of the street that is going in and out of that photograph and on which the motorbike is lying?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Mulamustafa Baseskija Street. Once upon a time it used to be called Marshal Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you later take a reverse angle of this view; in other words, looking another way along this street?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the usual procedure. You photograph a crime scene from both angles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we could see e-court page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is this, Officer, the reverse angle; in other words, looking back the way -- from the photograph that we saw before?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, later on, after taking these photographs, did you go up to the windows of a building and take some overhead photographs of the scene?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went up to the second floor of the building across the way from Markale, which is the building on the right-hand side of the photograph, and I took an overhead photograph of the entire street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: At this time I'll ask that e-court pages 3, 4 and 5 be displayed one after another to the witness, and then we will have a montage of 3, 4 and 5 that I will have a number of questions to put to the witness about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: We've just taken a look, Officer, at three photographs, e-court pages 3, 4 and 5. Did you put these photographs together to make one single large photograph of this crime scene as seen from overhead?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if I could ask, the montage of these photographs is on the ELMO. Could that be displayed, please. That's fine, thank you. And, Mr. President, for ease of presentation, we've also mounted this on -- this way, but I think that would be difficult to display in court. However, given the nature of the cross-examination of the preceding witness about things like shrapnel damage on buildings and blood on bicycles, we thought it important that this be presented in a large format. It will be available for the Chamber, but I intend to use the e-court presentation in questioning this witness. But we can switch to this at any time that the Chamber wishes to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: To begin with, sir, can you tell us where on this photograph the impact crater is seen?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And behind or between this impact crater --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't see the indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the witness to mark it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes, now I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just one second while we get a pen for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Sir, could you draw a circle around the impact crater on that photograph, please. Just label that IC for the English words, "impact crater."

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Between that impact crater and the wall of the building against which the two bicycles are leaning, were any portions of human bodies found by you and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, we found parts of human bodies, the lower extremities, most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you say "lower extremities," you mean feet and legs?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, is it significant to you as a forensic crime scene technician that what is found between the impact crater and the wall of that building are parts of the lower parts of human body rather than the upper parts?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is significant, the reason being, when the projectile landed the angle was closer to the ground. We can see the traces. It hits the ground and the shrapnel are sprayed very low down, which means that normally they hit people's legs or feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when the shrapnel -- if the shell comes in at an angle, is the shrapnel sprayed low to the ground in a complete circle around the point of impact, at only part of a circle around the point of impact; and if it's only part of the circle, could you tell us, please, which part of the circle?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: When a projectile lands, it always causes damage in the section that faces the direction from which it came. So this is the angle and this was the damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, in the area in front, as I will say, of the impact crater or the area towards your pen as you're holding it now, does the shrapnel come out low to the ground or not?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No, it goes up. It spreads upwards. In the photographs, you can see that the building across the way has sustained damage to its upper parts. In this photograph, you can see damage to the lower part of the Markale building itself, in addition to people's limbs being torn to bits. That's another thing that you can see in the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Docherty. You did ask the witness about his training and qualifications. I believe he said he took a six-month course in forensic matters. Was a part of this course the investigation of mortar shelling and craters?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'll ask. I doubt it, but I think that he will have an adequate foundation if I ask a different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I'd like to know how much experience he had prior to this in investigation of those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: To ask Judge Robinson's first question first: The six-month course that you took in 1987 when you became a crime scene technician, how much time of that six-month course, if any, was devoted to the analysis of explosions?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary, so we didn't do that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Where did you learn the things that you've just been testifying about, the way that shrapnel sprays out from an explosion? Where did you learn those things? How did you learn those things? Could you just summarise that for Their Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Well, given the fact that in 1992 we went to a lot of on-site investigations, there were many UN people who came with us. We learned a lot from them about the point of impact, about the type of shell. They helped us a great deal in determining the various directions from which these projectiles were arriving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea of how many investigations of this kind he would have carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That was my next question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How many shelling investigations had you been involved in before you went to Markale market in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I had been involved in between 30 and 40 of those, including the Markale 1 incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And as part of those investigations, was it part of the Sarajevo canton of the Ministry of the Interior's job to determine an angle at which a shell had come in, if that was possible?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was done by experts attached to the security services centre, which has now been renamed as the federal MUP. They would calculate the angle of descent of a given projectile. We didn't do that. That wasn't our job. Our job was to investigate a crime scene by taking photographs, by making sketches, by filming and by analysing evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can barely hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please speak into the microphone. The interpreters are not hearing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You say that this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: One question. [Interpretation] Just one question to clarify a point. We talked about Markale 1 and Markale 2. Those are two different incidents. The Markale 1 is the open market; is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So now, talking about the impact point, where were the people who were buying goods and the people selling goods? Were the stalls the day of the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean Markale 1 or Markale 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm actually asking you the question: Which Markale are we talking about here? This particular scene, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Markale 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the open market or the closed market?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Open air, both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Very well. Then in this particular market, I would like to know, where were the stalls? Where were the people buying goods and where were the people selling goods, with respect, of course, to the impact? Did the projectile fall amidst the people who were buying and selling or were they farther down? Because I imagine that the other market is approximately 200 metres from that point of impact, or from this market.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People were at the exit of the Markale market, this area over here. And the vendors were over here, to the left and to the right, people selling cigarettes and various goods. People were leaving, coming out this way. This is the exit. And they had the choice of heading left towards the Markale open market, which lies at a distance of some 150 metres from this spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Officer, is there damage, fresh damage, to the facade of the building against which the two bicycles are leaning?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. There's damage in the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you. I was going to ask you to circle -- if one was looking on the large photograph for that damage, could you just make some marks on this photograph where fresh shrapnel damage appears for -- as a key to where to look.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Precisely here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so this shrapnel damage, was it low down on the building or high up on the building?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This part of the wall is about 60 centimetres, which means up to 80 centimetres or 1 metre. But it's concentrated here, in this portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How does that pattern of shrapnel damage compare to the pattern of shrapnel damage on the building across the street?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: The building opposite had a lot of windows broken and also damage on the facade at about the height of 1 metre or 1.5 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, I understand you won't be able to give us a compass direction from which this shell may have come, but from the fact that the building against which the bicycles are leaning has shrapnel damage down low, the building across the street has shrapnel damage higher up, and that injuries to people between the impact crater and the building against which the bicycles are leaning were to their lower extremities, what, if anything, can we tell about the general direction from which this round came?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This shell came from the south towards north, so from the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Looking at the crater itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Court officer, if we could see page -- oh, excuse me. I will offer the marked-up document that is on the ELMO into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But is he going to explain the conclusion he has arrived at? Are you moving to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, I can. I had thought that I had done that by talking about the way in which the shrapnel comes out low and high, in different directions, but I can do it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I overlooked that, but that shouldn't be done because really that's leading on an important question. You should ask him -- to say "What direction did the shrapnel come from, and what is your reason for that," and then he would have provided all of the information that you provided in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, I believe that all of the information that I incorporated in the question was evidence which the witness had testified to in response to non-leading questions, and I was summing up only for the sake of clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: But let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would like to have him explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Officer, the conclusion that you just gave us, that the shell came from the south, can you explain your conclusion, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: The determination of the direction of a projectile is based on the impression or the trace left on the ground, and it's like this: The direction from which a shell is coming makes the trace in the form of a paw. At the point of explosion, shrapnel is released. It damages the asphalt or whatever. And by joining these two points, you draw a line and you arrive at the direction from which the shell came, because this is where the damage is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's very simple, and we had been shown how to do that by UN personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as Exhibit P261.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if we could please, then, move to e-court page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: On the monitor in front of you, Officer, there is a photograph. Is this one of the photographs that you took that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the centre of the explosion, marked with number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Who placed the number 1 in this scene?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And is this crater in exactly the same condition that it was immediately after the shell had landed or has it been changed; and if it's been changed, could you describe what's been done to Their Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's been changed, because there's a lot of rubble immediately after the explosion and we cannot make our determinations without clearing up the scene. After removal of the material, we arrived at this pattern of damage, based on which we determined the direction of this shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Has any part of the crater been outlined in chalk?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: The centre itself wasn't. Only these benchmarks were marked with chalk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Were those chalk markings made by a member of your team?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I cleared the scene, and a colleague of mine put these markings to facilitate the identification of the direction and to get a better photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I think you anticipated my next question, which was going to be: What was the purpose of making this chalk outline?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: As I said, in order to make it possible -- as much as possible, to determine the incoming direction. We mark all the visible points on the scene, that is, on asphalt in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, moving the rubble and making the chalk outline obviously has changed the appearance of the crater. But my question is: What effect, if any, has moving the rubble and making the chalk outline had on the actual gouges in the asphalt of the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned colleague was putting a leading question. He said that the removal of this rubble has affected changes. He should have asked this question in a different way. Nevertheless, he said that the removal of the rubble changed the picture, and I think this is a most leading question. He may just ask him what happened with this surface and this area after the intervention carried out by his team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question, as I see it, is: What effect, if any, has moving the rubble and making the chalk outline had on the actual gouges in the actual asphalt of the road? That's not leading. The witness may answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then the translation was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps. I pass no judgement on that. But the witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no major changes occurred, because this was a hard asphalt surface which suffered no major changes and alterations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we could see e-court page 22 of this ter number, please, Mr. Court Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And while that is coming up, Officer, I will ask: Was the stabiliser fin to a mortar grenade found at Markale market that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Was it near or far from the impact -- or how far was it from the impact crater, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Between 25 and 30 metres from the point of impact, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: We're now looking on the screen at e-court page 22. Is this a photograph that you took that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you see a number 9 and a number 12 that have been written on the photographic print?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What is the significance of the number 12?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Number 12 signifies the stabiliser fin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to take a look at some close-ups of this stabiliser fin, and that will be e-court pages 24, 25, 26, 27, and 28. If we could start with number 24, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is this a photograph that you took that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And does this show the stabiliser fin where it was found?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this number 12 on the small black board, what's the purpose of putting these objects at crime scenes, these numbered placards?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That's also a standard procedure. When all this physical evidence has to be collected and sent for examination, they are marked with numbers first. And here we also marked the extremities and the damage at the very entrance to the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if we could move to e-court page 26, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you take this photograph, Officer?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was taken against a ruler in order to give it the size, and these little fields are 1 centimetre each.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So just to clarify, each of those squares, whether black or white, is 1 centimetre in length.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Through your work in Sarajevo, did you become familiar with what a stabiliser fin to a mortar grenade looks like?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are three types, and after an impact -- could you please be more specific with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Certainly. Does this stabiliser fin appear to have suffered damage; and if the answer to that question is yes, could you specify what sort of damage this stabiliser fin has received?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Upon impact it approximate becomes damaged. In this particular case, the stabiliser was flattened probably by the cars that were passing by there, providing assistance to the wounded and the killed. So one part of it is flattened, as can you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you have just offered an explanation as to why the stabiliser fin was flattened. Can you offer any explanation as to why the stabiliser fin was located 25 to 30 metres from the point of impact?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Since at that moment there were many people offering assistance to the casualties, whether someone wanted to take it as a souvenir or whether it was just kind of pushed under the tires of the automobiles, it's difficult to say how it happened for it to be there where it was, at 25 to 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And now if we could see the last two photographs, please, e-court page 27 and e-court page 28. And then lastly e-court page 28, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. It was taken on the premises of the police station by a man working in the photo laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this photograph and the one immediately preceding it, do you note damage to the stabiliser fin of this mortar grenade?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And again, when you say "it's identical," are you talking about the flattening of the fins that you testified to a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If we could now move, please, to e-court 145A.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Officer, did you prepare a free-hand sketch of the crime scene that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What's the purpose of making a sketch?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: The purpose is to be able to reconstruct the event at any future point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: May I have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if we could see the third page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is what's on the monitor in front of you, Officer, the sketch that you drew that day?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the sketch of the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: There are a number of dimensions on that sketch. How are those measurements taken? And, in particular, what steps were taken to make sure that they were accurate?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: These measurements were taken from the building, the Markale building, from the left-hand side building to the right-hand side building, which constitutes about 10.5 metres' distance. That is where the impact point was. It was about 4 or 4.5 metres away from the wall of the building. Besides, these numbers signify body parts, bicycles, shoes. All the physical evidence found on the spot were photographed and marked with numbers. And the sketch is always part of a photo file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Who took --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can you ask the witness to identify the direction of north on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Which way is north on this map, Officer, on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Approximately, this is the northerly direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be maybe be useful to put N, Mr. President, because one might think that S means south. That could be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please put an N.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Before we mark this, can we tender the unmarked one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the unmarked will be admitted as Exhibit P262, and unfortunately we'll have to remark the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you show -- on this map, besides the dimensions, there are number of numbers with circles drawing around them. Is there any correspondence between the numbers in circles on this sketch and the numbers that we saw on the little black placards at the crime scene? If there is a correspondence, can you explain it to the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I was able to locate this document, I wasn't able to do so in the set of documents provided by the Prosecution. However, I have no objections. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But it may be a matter for concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document was turned over -- I'll check, but last week, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us proceed. If you have another occasion in which you can't find a document, bring it to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The question that was pending, Officer, was: On this chart there are a number of numbers inside little circles, and I'm asking if there's a correspondence between the numbers and the circles on this chart and the numbers on the -- the white numbers on the black placards that we saw in the photographs of the crime scene. If there is a correspondence, could you please explain it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: There is no correspondence. What has been done in the sketch corresponds to the photographs, and the markings are identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the word "correspondence" may not have been well chosen. But, for example, on the far left of the sketch, we see the number 12 circled. What was at number 12?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Number 12 was the stabiliser fin of the mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And earlier we saw the stabiliser shell on the pavement and a photograph of it taken, and there was one of those little placards beside it. What number was on the little placard in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Number 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the last two markings I'm going to ask you to make on this sketch are -- because the markings are quite small, could you show us, please, the impact crater.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And second of all, just for purposes of orientation, we saw some bicycles up against a wall in some earlier photographs. Can you show us approximately where those bicycles were so that people can correspond the sketch to the photographs.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just ask him, what condition were those bicycles in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't look at them, but one can see in the photographs whether these bicycles are damaged or not. But I myself cannot say that. There couldn't have been any damage, particularly because body parts of the people who had been there had absorbed most of the shrapnel. Therefore, these bicycles could have been protected by the victims' bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. We have to take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. Can I tender this before we take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P263, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
